stem: A team wants to find insecure coding patterns in source code early, before the application is even runnable. Which technique is BEST?

options.rationale: SAST analyzes source/bytecode without executing it, catching coding flaws early and pinpointing the affected lines.
DAST requires a running, deployable application and cannot run before the app is runnable.
Surveys do not analyze code for security flaws.
Physical audits are unrelated to source-code analysis.

stem: To find runtime and configuration issues by attacking a deployed, running web application from the outside, which technique is BEST?

options.rationale: DAST tests the running application externally, revealing runtime/config vulnerabilities and confirming exploitability.
SAST inspects source without running it, so it cannot observe runtime/deployment behavior.
Restore testing validates recovery, not application runtime security.
Fire drills are physical safety exercises, unrelated to app testing.

stem: Which statement MOST correctly contrasts SAST and DAST?

options.text: SAST analyzes source without running it (early); DAST tests the running app externally (later)
options.rationale: SAST is static/early/white-box; DAST is dynamic/later/black-box — the core distinction the exam tests.

options.text: SAST tests the running app; DAST analyzes source code
options.rationale: This reverses the two techniques.

options.text: Both require the application to be deployed and running
options.rationale: SAST does not require a running app; DAST does.
Both are effective at finding different classes of vulnerabilities.

stem: A known limitation of SAST that teams must manage is MOST accurately which of the following?

options.text: It tends to produce false positives that require triage
options.rationale: Static analysis commonly flags issues that are not truly exploitable, so results must be validated to avoid wasted effort.

options.text: It can only test a running, deployed application
options.rationale: That describes DAST; SAST works on source without running it.
SAST reports many findings; the challenge is filtering false positives.
SAST identifies issues; it does not auto-fix them.

stem: A tool instruments the running application to correlate a live request with the exact vulnerable code path, improving accuracy. This is MOST accurately which technique?

options.rationale: IAST instruments the running app to combine inside code knowledge with runtime behavior, improving accuracy over SAST or DAST alone.
Pure DAST lacks the internal instrumentation that links runtime to specific code paths.
SAST does not execute the app, so it cannot correlate live requests to code at runtime.
This is unrelated to application security testing.

stem: 'Shifting security left' in the SDLC MOST directly means which of the following?

options.text: Performing security testing earlier in development to catch issues sooner and cheaper
options.rationale: Shift-left moves testing earlier so defects are found and fixed before they become costly in later stages.

options.text: Only testing after the product is retired
options.rationale: Testing at end-of-life is the opposite of shifting left.
Shift-left increases early testing, not eliminates it.

options.text: Moving the code repository to a different server
options.rationale: Shift-left concerns timing of testing, not repo location.

stem: To identify known-vulnerable third-party libraries used by an application, which technique is BEST?

options.rationale: SCA specifically inventories and flags known vulnerabilities in third-party/open-source dependencies.
Fuzzing finds input-handling crashes, not known-vulnerable dependencies.
Physical audits do not analyze software dependencies.
Surveys do not identify vulnerable libraries.

stem: A manager wants the most complete application-security assurance. What is the BEST strategy?

options.text: Layer multiple techniques (SAST, DAST, SCA, manual review) since none finds everything
options.rationale: Each method has blind spots; combining static, dynamic, dependency, and manual analysis provides the broadest coverage.

options.text: Rely solely on SAST and skip everything else
options.rationale: SAST alone misses runtime/config and dependency issues.

options.text: Rely solely on a single DAST scan
options.rationale: DAST alone misses source-level and dependency issues.

options.text: Do no testing to save time
options.rationale: Skipping testing provides no assurance.

stem: Assessing an application's database security MOST importantly includes checking for which of the following?

options.text: SQL injection exposure, excessive account privileges, and inference/aggregation risks
options.rationale: Database security assessment focuses on injection exposure, over-privileged accounts, and confidentiality risks like inference/aggregation.

options.text: The color of the database console
options.rationale: Console color is irrelevant to database security.
Physical aesthetics do not affect database security posture.
Personal preferences are not a security assessment criterion.

stem: Fuzzing primarily helps find which type of software weakness?

options.text: Input-handling flaws revealed by malformed or unexpected input
options.rationale: Fuzzing sends malformed/random input to trigger crashes and expose input-handling vulnerabilities.
Fuzzing is a software technique, not a physical assessment.
Lighting is unrelated to fuzzing.
Elevators are unrelated to software fuzzing.

stem: Which technique can generally be applied EARLIEST in the development process?

options.text: SAST, because it analyzes source code without needing a running app
options.rationale: SAST works on source/bytecode before the app is runnable, so it fits earliest in the SDLC.

options.text: DAST, because it needs a deployed running app
options.rationale: DAST requires a deployable, running application, so it comes later than SAST.
Pen testing a live system occurs late, after deployment.
RUM requires live production users, the latest stage.

stem: A live application leaks stack traces via verbose error pages only when running. Which technique is MOST likely to catch this?

options.text: DAST, which tests the running application and observes runtime responses
options.rationale: A runtime-only issue like verbose error output is best found by DAST probing the live app, not by static source analysis.

options.text: SAST, which never runs the app
options.rationale: SAST cannot observe runtime behavior like error-page output.
SCA finds vulnerable libraries, not runtime error-handling behavior.
Restore testing is unrelated to application runtime behavior.

stem: Which technique MOST directly helps developers by pinpointing the exact line of vulnerable source code?

options.rationale: Because SAST analyzes source, it can point developers to the specific line/file needing a fix.
DAST tests from outside and usually cannot identify the exact source line.
Guard patrols are unrelated to source code.
Surveys do not locate source-code flaws.

stem: What can skilled manual code review find that automated scanners MOST often miss?

options.text: Complex business-logic flaws that require human understanding of intent
options.rationale: Automated tools struggle with logic flaws that depend on business context; human reviewers can reason about intent.
Manual review catches logic flaws automation misses, so this is false.
Manual security review targets logic/security flaws, not merely typos.
Power usage is unrelated to code review.

stem: IAST is best described as which of the following?

options.text: A technique that instruments the running app to combine runtime testing with internal code visibility
options.rationale: IAST uses instrumentation inside the running application to blend dynamic testing with code-level insight for accuracy.

options.text: A purely static scan of source only
options.rationale: That is SAST; IAST involves the running, instrumented app.

options.text: A physical penetration of a building
options.rationale: IAST is software testing, not physical intrusion.
IAST tests application security, not backups.

stem: Why does shifting security testing left MOST benefit the organization economically?

options.text: Defects found earlier are cheaper to fix than those found in production
options.rationale: The cost to remediate rises sharply the later a defect is found, so early detection saves money and rework.

options.text: Early testing makes bugs more expensive to fix
options.rationale: Early detection lowers, not raises, remediation cost.

options.text: It eliminates the need to fix bugs at all
options.rationale: Bugs still require fixing; shifting left just finds them sooner.
Earlier detection has a clear cost benefit.

stem: What is a prerequisite MOST specific to running a DAST scan?

options.text: A deployable, running instance of the application to test against
options.rationale: DAST exercises the live application, so it needs a running instance, unlike SAST which uses source.
DAST needs a running target; it is not requirement-free.

options.text: The application to be permanently offline
options.rationale: An offline app cannot be dynamically tested.
Deleting source is irrelevant and harmful; DAST needs a running app, not source removal.

stem: A SAST tool flagged a possible injection, but the team wants to confirm whether it is actually exploitable in the running app. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use DAST or a targeted penetration test against the running application
options.rationale: Dynamic testing/pen testing exercises the live app to confirm whether the flagged issue is truly exploitable.

options.text: Assume every SAST finding is automatically exploitable
options.rationale: SAST produces false positives; assuming all are exploitable wastes effort.
Blindly deleting code is not a validation method.
Ignoring a flagged injection risks leaving a real vulnerability unaddressed.

stem: To keep application security assurance current as code changes frequently, what is BEST?

options.text: Integrate automated security testing (SAST/DAST/SCA) into the CI/CD pipeline to run on changes
options.rationale: Continuous, automated testing on each change keeps assurance current in fast-moving development.

options.text: Test only once at project kickoff
options.rationale: A single early test becomes stale as code evolves.

options.text: Never test after the first release
options.rationale: Ongoing changes reintroduce risk that requires continued testing.

options.text: Rely on users to report all vulnerabilities
options.rationale: Relying on users is reactive and misses many issues.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant to assessing software security effectiveness?

options.text: The font used in the application's source-code comments
options.rationale: Comment font has no bearing on whether the software's security controls are effective, making it least relevant.

options.text: SAST results on the source code
options.rationale: SAST findings directly inform software security assessment.

options.text: DAST results on the running app
options.rationale: DAST results reveal runtime security issues, highly relevant.
Dependency vulnerabilities are a key part of the assessment.
